mcqs.question: In a React Native FlatList, tapping a row updates selectedId in parent state, but the previously selected row never visually deselects. data did not change. Why?
options: FlatList is a PureComponent: values outside data that affect rendering must arrive through changed props, so pass extraData={selectedId}
The list needs getItemLayout so rows re-render at the new selection
keyExtractor must include the selection state so each row gets a fresh key
Each row must be wrapped in React.memo with default props
mcqs.explanation: Correct: FlatList is a PureComponent, so a re-render only happens when its props change; selection lives outside data, so it must be passed as extraData (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/docs/flatlist). The strongest distractor is option 3: baking selection into keys does force an update, but keys are identity, so every affected row remounts, losing row state and animations instead of updating in place.

mcqs.question: A team porting a web app to React Native assumes their existing DOM manipulation and CSS will keep working. Which statement reflects React Native's actual rendering model?
options: React components describe the UI, but core components map to native platform views, not browser DOM elements, so web CSS and browser APIs cannot be assumed to exist
The app renders inside a system web view, so existing DOM code keeps working after a small polyfill
React components are compiled to native source code at build time, so there is no JavaScript at runtime
The browser DOM is emulated on top of native views, so most web APIs work with minor differences
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the JavaScript side contains components and application logic while native projects bundle that JavaScript and render native components, so a web CSS or browser API must never be assumed (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/docs/components-and-apis). The strongest distractor is option 2: it describes a web-view approach, not React Native, whose core components map to real native views.

mcqs.question: After migrating to React Native's New Architecture, a team is surprised that startup time did not improve. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Serialization over the old bridge was probably not their bottleneck, and the app may need refactoring to benefit; the New Architecture enables capabilities rather than guaranteeing speedups
The migration was incomplete: JSI benefits require rewriting the components in C++
The old bridge is still running in parallel and must be deleted manually
Startup is always dominated by the bridge, so the measurement itself must be wrong
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the official guidance warns that an app may need refactoring and that serialization may not have been its bottleneck, so JSI-based interop and Fabric are capabilities, not automatic performance wins (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/architecture/landing-page). The strongest distractor is option 4: it denies the measurement instead of questioning the assumption, and it is exactly the belief that led the team to expect a guaranteed speedup.

mcqs.question: A team using Expo Go for daily development needs to integrate a third-party native library. What is the recommended move?
options: Move from Expo Go to a development build, which can include native libraries and production-like behavior
Eject to bare React Native immediately, because Expo cannot use native modules
Stay on Expo Go and mock the native library in development
Rebuild the app natively in Swift and Kotlin
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Expo Go is a limited playground, not the production development environment, so the move is a development build when native libraries or production-like behavior matter (Expo: https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/overview/). The strongest distractor is option 2: it is the classic eject myth; needing a native library is a limitation of the playground, not of the toolchain, and an Expo app is still a React Native app.

mcqs.question: What submission format does Google Play use for new app releases, and what does it do?
options: Android App Bundle: you upload the signed bundle and Play generates device-optimized APKs from it
A universal APK containing every density and architecture
An IPA package signed with the upload key
A signed release APK; App Bundles are optional and only for large teams
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Google Play uses Android App Bundles to generate device-optimized APKs, and requires signing (Google Play: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859152). The strongest distractor is option 2: a universal APK is what internal testing builds produce, but shipping it to the store sends every device all code and assets and does not match Play's submission requirements.

mcqs.question: A web developer ports a card component to React Native: a CSS grid rule, `1rem` padding, a `fontSize` declared on the wrapping container, and a `.card--active` modifier class toggled by state. Which statement describes what React Native actually supports?
options: `StyleSheet.create` turns the objects into scoped, CSS-like rules, so the `.card--active` modifier resolves by name instead of by array position.
Typography and color declared on a parent `<View>` inherit into nested `<Text>` elements, so the container-level font size keeps working after the port.
Styles are plain objects merged left to right on the `style` prop: there are no selectors or cascade, `flexDirection` defaults to `column`, and numeric sizes are density-independent pixels.
Percentage widths resolve against the device screen, so `width: '50%'` behaves like CSS `50vw` on every phone.
mcqs.explanation: React Native styles are JavaScript objects passed through the `style` prop; arrays merge left to right with later entries winning, so the modifier is just a second object in the array, and `flexDirection` defaults to `column` instead of CSS's `row` (https://reactnative.dev/docs/style, https://reactnative.dev/docs/flexbox). The strongest distractor is option 0: `StyleSheet.create` looks like the CSS-modules entry point, but it registers styles and returns them; it creates no scopes and no class names, so nothing is ever resolved by name. Option 1 imports CSS inheritance, but text styles inherit only from a `<Text>` ancestor, not from a `<View>`. Option 3 is the reverse of the documented rule: percentages resolve against the parent's size, not the screen.

mcqs.question: Deep links open the right screen while the app is running, but the same URL tapped from a cold start leaves the app on the initial route. The code registers `Linking.addEventListener('url', handler)` inside a component effect and navigates from that handler. What is the actual gap?
options: The listener subscribes too late: registering it before `AppRegistry.registerComponent` makes React Native replay the initial URL as a normal event.
The OS strips query parameters from the URL during a cold start, so the handler receives a link it cannot match and ignores it.
A cold start needs its own prefix, for example `example-cold://`, because the normal scheme is only registered once the app has already run.

A cold start delivers the URL once as the initial URL, which the listener never sees because it is not a `url` event; that path must be read and turned into navigation state, or delegated to `NavigationContainer`'s `linking`, which handles both entry points.
mcqs.explanation: Deep linking has two entry points: the initial URL that launched the app and the URL events that arrive while it runs. `NavigationContainer` with `linking` covers both; a hand-rolled solution has to call `Linking.getInitialURL()` in addition to subscribing (https://reactnavigation.org/docs/deep-linking). The strongest distractor is option 0: it notices the real symptom, that the subscription happens after the URL already arrived, but proposes a mechanism that does not exist. No registration order turns the launch URL into an event; it is a separate source, and moving `addEventListener` earlier leaves the cold start just as broken. Option 1 invents parameter stripping, since the platform hands over the full URL. Option 2 invents a second scheme; the custom scheme is declared once in the native configuration, not per launch mode.

mcqs.question: A progress bar animates `width` through `Animated.timing` and stutters whenever the JS thread is busy. A teammate changes the config to `useNativeDriver: true` and the bar stops animating, with React Native reporting that the style property is not supported by the native animated module. What is the correct reading?
options: Interpolate the value into the width output range and keep `useNativeDriver: true`: interpolation math runs on the native side, so the layout property becomes native-driven too.

The native driver only animates non-layout properties such as `opacity` and `transform`; a bar driven by `width` needs the JS driver, a `transform: [{ scaleX }]` rewrite, or a UI-thread style if the JS thread must stay free.
Set `isInteraction: false` on the animation: layout properties are only excluded from the native driver while the animation holds an interaction handle.
It is a development-only guard; a release build lets the native driver animate every style property.
mcqs.explanation: The native driver sends the whole animation to native before it starts, so it runs without the JS thread and without driving layout: you can animate non-layout properties such as `transform` and `opacity`, not flexbox or position properties (https://reactnative.dev/docs/animations). The strongest distractor is option 0 because it is half right: interpolation does execute natively for supported values, which makes the reasoning sound convincing, but the limit is the property the animation finally writes, not where the interpolation runs, and `width` stays a layout property. Option 2 confuses `isInteraction`, which controls whether the animation registers an interaction handle so lists can defer work, with driver support. Option 3 invents a build-mode gate that does not exist.

mcqs.question: Only low-end Android users report dropped frames while scrolling the feed. A React Native DevTools performance trace shows the JS thread mostly idle and short React commits during the scroll, while the in-app Perf Monitor FPS number still drops. What is the correct next step?
options: Take it to the platform profiler (Android Studio Profiler or a Perfetto system trace) on a physical device with a release-like build, because JS-idle jank is layout, drawing, image or view-count work that DevTools cannot attribute.
Throttle the CPU in DevTools and re-read the JS flame chart: a high enough multiplier turns a laptop into the low-end device and reproduces the dropped frames.
Memoize the rows and raise `windowSize`, because an idle JS thread means React work is still happening outside the profiler's sampling window.
Use the Perf Monitor FPS reading as the release measurement, since it renders the same JavaScript bundle users run.
mcqs.explanation: The debugging split is by substrate: DevTools covers JavaScript concerns such as console, breakpoints, component inspection, the React Profiler, network events, performance traces and memory snapshots, while frame cost on the native side belongs to the platform profilers, and jank should be reproduced on a physical device with Development Mode off (https://reactnative.dev/docs/debugging, https://reactnative.dev/docs/profiling). The strongest distractor is option 1: CPU throttling is a legitimate lab technique, but throttling the JS thread cannot attribute work that the trace already places outside the JS thread, and a dev build's extra instrumentation changes what is being measured. Option 2 prescribes JS-side fixes for a JS-idle profile, and raising `windowSize` mounts more rows. Option 3 promotes a diagnostic overlay into a measurement.

scenarios.prompt: Users report two bugs in this list: (1) tapping a row updates selection on some rows but the previously selected row often stays highlighted, and (2) after a fast scroll, the list lands on the wrong message. Row bodies can wrap to two or three lines. Explain both bugs and fix the component.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Bug 1 is a PureComponent prop problem. FlatList is a PureComponent, so it only re-renders when its props change. Tapping a row changes selectedId in the parent, but data does not change, so from the list's perspective nothing it watches has changed and rows keep stale selection visuals. The fix is to pass the outside value as a changed prop: extraData={selectedId}. Do not fix it by baking selection into keyExtractor: keys are identity, and changing them remounts rows, destroying row state and animations. While here, also stabilize renderItem and row props: the inline closure and the inline onPress are recreated every render, which works against keeping unrelated state from redrawing cells; hoist renderItem or memoize it and pass a stable onPress callback. Bug 2 is a geometry contract violation. getItemLayout is only valid for fixed-size rows: it lets the list skip measurement by trusting the declared length and offset. Row bodies wrap to two or three lines, so real heights exceed 64, and every offset after a tall row is wrong; the list scrolls to computed positions that no longer match content, which shows up as landing on the wrong message. Either constrain rows to a true fixed height (for example, clamped or truncated bodies) or remove getItemLayout and let the list measure. Before tuning anything else, profile to confirm where the time actually goes, and validate the fix on a representative lower-end Android device rather than a simulator, because window sizes tuned on a simulator can blank content on real devices or waste memory.
rubric: Diagnoses bug 1 through FlatList being a PureComponent and fixes it with extraData, not key hacks
Diagnoses bug 2 as getItemLayout's fixed-geometry contract being violated by variable-height rows
Keeps renderItem and row props stable instead of recreating closures each render
Profiles before tuning knobs and adjusts windowing only against device measurements
Validates on a representative lower-end Android device, not only a simulator

scenarios.prompt: A teammate flipped `useNativeDriver` from `false` to `true` to fix a stuttering progress bar. Now the bar never animates and React Native reports that the style property is not supported by the native animated module. The `addListener`-to-`setState` wiring is still there, `progress` is a 0-1 fraction, and the component can unmount mid-animation. Predict what happens in each case, explain why, and rewrite the component so its frames no longer depend on the JS thread.
rubric: Predicts failure at start, not slow frames: the animation never begins because `width` (including its interpolation to a percentage) is a layout property the native driver cannot run.
Identifies the per-frame `setState` listener as the stutter in the JS-driver build, and explains that a React commit per frame ties the bar to JS-thread availability.
Rewrites with a non-layout property (`transform: [{ scaleX }]`) on the native driver, or a UI-thread style for the width case, and removes the listener from the render path.
Cleans up the animation and listener on unmount and on `progress` changes, and keeps one driver per `Animated.Value`.
States a verification method - JS deliberately blocked, profile on a physical release-like build - and keeps business and accessibility state on JS instead of per frame.

scenarios.prompt: Marketing sends two links: `example://feed` and `https://app.example.com/users/42`. The first opens the app but lands on Home instead of the Feed tab; the second opens the browser. The linking config below is the entire JavaScript-side setup. Explain both failures, rewrite the contract, and list what has to change outside the JavaScript bundle for the https link to reach the app.
rubric: Names the nesting mismatch as the cause of the Home landing: `Feed` sits inside `Home`, so the URL matches no screen and the container falls back to its initial route; the fix mirrors the tree and adds a wildcard.

Separates the two https failures: the missing prefix is a JavaScript parsing gap, while the domain association (Associated Domains and AASA on iOS, autoVerify and Digital Asset Links on Android) is decided by the OS before JS runs.
Treats URL parameters as untrusted input: validates `:id` before fetching and types the param list.
Keeps a single deep-link owner so cold start and foreground events do not double-navigate, using the `getInitialURL`/`subscribe` overrides when other sources exist.
Describes verification on both platforms including a cold start, and states the installed-app limit of universal links.
